rulesetReview.currentText: Nine players take the field. A standard game has nine innings; each team bats once per inning until three outs are recorded.
rulesetReview.note: Consistent with general knowledge of OBR, but the rulebook was not opened. Levels differ: many youth and some WBSC/MiLB competitions play 7-inning games. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: Four balls give the batter a walk to first base. Three strikes is a strikeout. A foul ball counts as a strike unless the batter already has two strikes (a foul bunt with two strikes is a strikeout).
rulesetReview.note: Snippets of OBR Definition of Terms (Strike) and 5.09(a) agree: foul with <2 strikes is a strike; bunted foul is a strike on any count. Suggest adding: a foul tip legally caught by the catcher is a strike even with two strikes (third strike = out). search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: Roughly the area over home plate from the midpoint between the batter's shoulders and belt down to the hollow below the kneecap, based on the batter's stance as they swing.
rulesetReview.note: Snippet of OBR definition: upper limit is the midpoint between the top of the shoulders and the top of the uniform pants; lower limit the hollow beneath the kneecap; judged from the stance as the batter is prepared to swing. Suggested wording: '...top of the shoulders and the top of the uniform pants... judged from the batter's stance as they prepare to swing'. Note MLB's 2026 ABS challenge system uses its own zone dimensions (not verified). search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: Common ways to be out: strikeout, a batted ball caught in the air, being tagged with the ball while off a base, or a force out at a base.
rulesetReview.note: Plausible summary; not verified against OBR 5.09 text. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: A batted ball that lands or is played in fair territory is in play; balls outside the foul lines are foul.
rulesetReview.section: Definitions: Fair Ball / Foul Ball (not opened)
rulesetReview.note: Oversimplified: under OBR definitions, ground balls are judged by where they are when passing first/third base or when they settle/are touched; fly balls by where they first land beyond the bases; foul lines and poles are fair. Could not confirm exact wording. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: Runners must touch each base in order. Only one runner may occupy a base. On a caught fly ball, runners must tag up before advancing.
rulesetReview.note: Plausible; tag-up applies to any legally caught fly ball (retouch original base after the catch is first touched). Not verified. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: A run scores when a runner legally touches all four bases before the third out (a run doesn't count if the third out is a force out or the batter-runner is out before reaching first).
rulesetReview.note: Snippet of OBR 5.08(a) lists a third exception the app omits: no run scores if the third out is a preceding runner declared out for failing to touch a base (appeal). Suggested addition. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: With runners on first and second (or bases loaded) and fewer than two outs, an easily catchable infield pop-up is declared an infield fly and the batter is out, to stop the defence deliberately dropping it for a double play.
rulesetReview.note: Snippets of OBR definition agree on runners and outs; add that it must be a FAIR fly ball (not a line drive or attempted bunt) catchable by an infielder with ordinary effort; runners may advance at their own risk. search snippet only; source not opened

rulesetReview.currentText: Many leagues, including MLB, allow a designated hitter to bat in place of the pitcher.
rulesetReview.note: News reports: MLB adopted the universal DH in 2022 (both leagues), with a two-way-player provision letting a starting pitcher who is also the DH stay in as DH after leaving the mound. Rulebook number (5.11) not confirmed. search snippet only; source not opened

newRulePoints.text: UNVERIFIED (search snippet only): In MLB the pitcher has 15 s to begin the delivery with bases empty and 18 s with runners on (18 s since 2024). Pitchers get two disengagements (step-offs/pickoffs) per plate appearance; an unsuccessful third advances runners one base. Amateur levels may differ.

UNVERIFIED (news report): From 2026 MLB umpires still call every pitch, but each team may challenge ball/strike calls to the automated system, starting with two per game; a successful challenge is retained. Applies to MLB only.

UNVERIFIED (snippet): WBSC competitions use the WBSC Official Rules of Baseball 2025-2026 edition; reported changes include 120-second pitching changes/inning breaks (except U-12 World Cup) and pitch-clock sanctions without prior warning.

UNVERIFIED: Many professional and international competitions start extra innings with a runner placed on second base (MLB, WBC); WBSC Olympic baseball has used runners on first and second. Check your competition rules.

claims.statement: Pitch Smart daily pitch maximums (per secondary snippets): ages 7-8: 50, 9-10: 75, 11-12: 85, 13-16: 95, 17-18: 105. These are recommendations; Little League's own limits are mandatory rules.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Snippet of Pitch Smart table for ages 9-14: 1-20 pitches = 0 rest days, 21-35 = 1, 36-50 = 2, 51-65 = 3, 66+ = 4. Older age bands use higher thresholds; sources disagree on the 17-18 top tiers.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Pitch Smart (per snippet): no youth pitcher should pitch three consecutive days regardless of count, nor pitch in more than one game in a day.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Pitch Smart (per snippet): at least 4 months a year off throwing, with 2-3 months continuous; ages 9-12 cap of 80 innings in 12 months; avoid pitching more than 8 months/year.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Pitch Smart (per snippet) advises youth players not to pitch and catch in the same game.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Systematic review of adolescent players identified arm fatigue, playing for multiple teams, pitch velocity, age and height as independent risk factors for throwing-arm injury; evidence for months/yr, innings/yr and GIRD was inconclusive.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: A study of tournament teams reported Pitch Smart non-compliance in over 90% of teams and about half of pitchers - coaches should actively track counts.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: A 2025 systematic review (8 small, heterogeneous studies) reported gains in rotator cuff strength, scapular stability and shoulder ROM from the Thrower's Ten; evidence for velocity gains is weak.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Little League Rule 7.08(a)(4) (per snippet): in Majors division and below, a runner sliding head-first while advancing is out; diving back to a base is allowed.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

claims.statement: Pitch Smart-based summaries suggest delaying breaking pitches until fastball and changeup command is consistent; one summary cites ~age 13-14 for curveballs. Exact official wording not confirmed.
claims.section: search snippet only; source not opened

safetyReview.currentText: Youth pitchers: follow Pitch Smart's age-based pitch counts and required rest days, and avoid pitching for multiple teams at once.
safetyReview.section: Pitch Smart age pages (not opened; snippets consistent; multiple teams supported as risk factor by s9 snippet)

safetyReview.currentText: Track every pitch and respect age-based pitch counts and rest days (Pitch Smart).
Young pitchers should master the fastball and changeup before breaking pitches.
Never throw through elbow or shoulder pain — stop and get assessed.
safetyReview.section: not opened; arm fatigue/pain history are reported risk factors

safetyReview.currentText: Build throwing volume gradually at the start of a season with a structured throwing progression.
Always wear a batting helmet when batting or running the bases; catchers wear full protective gear.
Sliding: learn feet-first slides under supervision; head-first sliding is restricted in many youth leagues.
safetyReview.section: Little League Rule 7.08(a)(4) per snippet: head-first slide while advancing prohibited in Majors and below

safetyReview.currentText: Keep a safe distance from swinging bats; use protective screens for batting practice pitchers.
Children should play multiple positions and other sports. Pitch counts and rest days for young pitchers are essential — see Pitch Smart.
